name: Crushed-flower blush

lead: Crushed-flower blush is cheek and lip colour made from plants: safflower petals, mulberries, strawberries, beet juice or similar, pressed or mashed and dabbed on. It gives the skin a pink-to-red flush that reads as health and youth.
It is among the oldest cosmetics. Safflower rouge is documented in China, and Greek and later European makers used crushed fruit and plant dyes. Modern natural-blush recipes revive the idea.

paras: Practitioners press the colour from petals or fruit, or blend plant powder into a cream or balm, then pat it onto the apple of the cheeks. Plant stains are sheer, so colour builds in layers and may fade through the day.

Plant colours are generally regarded as milder than the lead and cinnabar rouges used historically, but fresh-made products can stain unevenly, fade, or irritate sensitive skin; allergy to a particular plant is possible.

angle.text: The pigment tints the skin directly, adding colour to the cheeks. Sheer plant stains give a natural-looking flush that is built up in layers.

lead: Crushed-flower blush is cheek colour made by extracting pigment from petals, berries or roots and applying it as a stain, paste or powder. It adds a warm flush to the cheeks, which people use to make a face look healthier, livelier or more youthful [1][2].

Plant-based rouge has a long history. In China rouge from safflower is traced to the Shang dynasty; in ancient Greece makeup was made from crushed mulberries, beet juice, strawberries or red amaranth; and in 1825 a British beauty manual listed safflower, red sandalwood, Brazil wood and carmine among rouge ingredients [1][2]. Some historical rouges were far less benign, such as the lead-based and cinnabar pigments of Rome [1].
No clinical studies have examined homemade flower blush; its use is documented in historical and cosmetic-history sources.

paras: Rouge appears in ancient Egyptian art, where ground red ochre mixed with fat was used [1][2]. Greek men and women stained their cheeks with crushed mulberries, beet juice or strawberries [1], and Chinese rouge was made from safflower juice [1]. In fifteenth-century Italy, Caterina Sforza's recipe book included a red sandalwood rouge said to last eight days [2].

In the Victorian era, when visible makeup was frowned upon, women privately pinched their cheeks or dabbed on beet juice before meeting suitors [2]. Carmine, from cochineal insects, entered European rouge after the Spanish conquest of the Americas [2].
Modern natural-makeup recipes use petals, beet or hibiscus powders blended with a base. Plant stains tend to be sheer and may fade, so users often layer them.
